title: Was anything ever born?
hookLine: seed or sprout, chicken or egg? Gaudapada answers that nothing was ever truly born, and no one truly bound
carry: ajati: no one was ever truly bound
tomorrow: Emptying the sea with a blade of grass
last: THE MANDUKYA KARIKA: ROPE OR SNAKE?

cards: The argument starts over dessert. Which came first, the chicken or the egg? Somebody says the chicken, obviously; something had to lay it.
Somebody else says the egg, obviously; the chicken hatched from one. An uncle says it's a trick question. Nobody wins, and everybody has a good time.

Thinkers in India argued over the same kind of loop with a seed and a sprout: the seed makes the sprout, the sprout makes the seed. Gaudapada picks up that puzzle in the Mandukya Karika. But he doesn't pick a side.
He asks whether anything was ever really born at all.

teach.b: The word is ajati. Jati means birth; a-jati means no birth, non-origination. Here's how Gaudapada gets there.
Try to explain how something comes to be. Does it come from something that already exists? Then it didn't really come to be; it was already there.
Does it come from what doesn't exist at all?

teach.h: NOT FROM BEING, NOT FROM NOTHING.
teach.b: Nothing comes from nothing. Cause and effect chasing each other, like seed and sprout, never find a first beginning. So, he says, the wise don't affirm birth.

teach.h: NO ONE BOUND, NO ONE FREED.
teach.b: Then a stark verse: there is no dissolution and no origination; no one bound, no one striving, no one seeking freedom, no one freed. That, he says, is the highest truth. It can sound cold the first time.
No one freed, after all this seeking? But look at it from yesterday's path. When the rope is seen, the snake isn't killed.
Nothing is destroyed, nothing is saved; the danger was simply never born.

Gaudapada also says why the scriptures describe creation at all: stories of the world coming forth, like sparks from a fire or pots from clay, lead the mind toward the truth; they aren't the last word on it.
That's a bold claim, and it's his. Some other Vedanta schools hold that creation is real, that the Lord truly brings the world forth, and they answer him with care. So why would a Hindu seeker care?
The goal of the path is moksha, freedom. On Gaudapada's reading, moksha isn't something new you manufacture, a prize born on the day you finally earn it.
If no one was ever truly bound, freedom is recognizing what was always so.

how: Students of Advaita Vedanta meet Gaudapada's teaching of ajati by reading the Karika, often with a teacher and with Shankara's commentary.

games.q: the chicken or the egg, the seed or the sprout. you're Gaudapada. how do you answer?
o: ask whether anything was ever truly born.
games.why: he follows cause and effect until no first beginning can be found, and teaches ajati, no birth.

practice: Let the mind be as it is, and when a thought appears, a plan, a memory, a tune, gently ask: where did it start? Don't chase an answer; just look for its first moment, then let it go and wait for the next.
If you pray, rest in what was here before any thought.

wordCard.voice: The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, carrying his teaching of ajati: on his reading, nothing at all is ever truly born.

orig.note: Sanskrit: no birth, non-origination; Gaudapada's teaching that nothing is truly born.

carryVoice: Your line: ajati: no one was ever truly bound. On Gaudapada's reading, freedom is seeing what was always so. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mandukya Karika 2.32 (no dissolution, no origination, none bound, none striving, none seeking liberation, none liberated: the highest truth)
Mandukya Karika 3.15 (creation taught through clay, iron, sparks and the like as a means of leading the mind)
Mandukya Karika 4.3–4.4 and 4.14–4.23 (nothing born from the existent or the non-existent; the wise do not affirm birth; cause and effect, seed and sprout, without a first beginning)
